Chapter 5 — When New Evidence Arrives

Inference and Intervention | BK Advisors

Matthew Luke Kuch | BK Advisors

2026-04-11

Meet Hiwot

Hiwot, 47, regional health director, Amhara Region, Ethiopia (a composite drawn from Federal Ministry of Health quarterly reports — the details are real, the name is not)

It is Monday morning. Hiwot opens her email.

The latest quarterly report from one of her districts shows maternal deaths jumped from 9 last quarter to 14 this quarter — a 56% increase (consistent with FMOH district-level reporting trends).

Her phone is already ringing.

The question: What is the most likely explanation — and how should new evidence arriving over the next two weeks change her answer?

And here is the puzzle

Three explanations sit on the table within an hour:

  • The new district hospital lost two midwives. (Personnel attrition.)
  • A measles outbreak is overwhelming the inpatient ward. (Surge.)
  • The district just started reporting deaths it had been quietly missing. (Reporting improvement.)

They cannot all be the main story. But Hiwot does not yet know which is. Worse — different evidence will arrive in a different order, and her belief has to update each time.

How belief actually works

Start with what you already believe

Before any new evidence arrives, Hiwot has an opinion — based on history, on her sense of the district, on her knowledge of the staffing situation.

She thinks the three explanations are roughly equally likely: about 33 out of 100 for each. That is her starting belief.

We call this the prior. It is just a fancy word for “what I believed before the new evidence arrived.”

Then evidence arrives

Tuesday. The chief of staff at the district hospital calls. The two midwives are real — they did leave. But she also confirms there has been no unusual measles activity this quarter.

Two pieces of information at once. One makes “personnel attrition” more likely. The other makes “measles surge” less likely.

Hiwot updates.

Counts, not formulas

Out of her 100 mental “scenarios”, here is how the picture moves:

Before Tuesday After Tuesday
Personnel 33 55
Measles 33 8
Reporting 33 37
Total 100 100

The numbers shifted. Nobody changed Hiwot’s mind for her. The new facts made some scenarios more plausible and others less plausible, and the totals always still add to 100.

What just happened, in one sentence

Bayesian updating is just this: when new evidence arrives, you redistribute your “out of 100” between the explanations — keeping the total at 100 — based on which explanations the evidence fits.

That is the entire idea. There is no formula you need to memorise. There is just this redistribution rule, applied carefully.

Information flows along the picture

The picture decides where evidence flows

Hiwot’s three explanations live on a picture. Each explanation has its own boxes and arrows. New evidence enters the picture at one box — and spreads outward along the arrows.

This is why we drew the picture in Chapters 2 and 3. The picture tells you which boxes the new evidence is allowed to update — and which boxes it is not.

Three rules for how evidence flows

  1. Along a chain, evidence flows freely. New evidence about a midstream box updates everything upstream and downstream.
  2. Across a fork, evidence flows freely until you observe the parent. Once you know the parent, the two children become independent.
  3. Across a collider, evidence does not flow — unless you observe the collider, in which case it suddenly does.

Rule 3 is the strange one we warned you about in Chapter 2. We will see it bite in Chapter 6.

Hiwot’s most useful trick — explaining away

Wednesday. A second piece of evidence: the district HMIS officer confirms that the reporting pipeline was indeed cleaned up last quarter, and 4 of this quarter’s 14 deaths had been previously unrecorded.

explaining away

The reporting explanation just got more likely. And — this is the strange bit — the personnel explanation got less likely, even though no new evidence about personnel arrived.

Because if reporting is suddenly carrying more of the rise, less of the rise needs to be carried by anything else.

This is called explaining away. One cause becoming more likely automatically makes its competitors less likely — even without new evidence about them.

The picture after explaining away

Before Wednesday After Wednesday
Personnel 55 32
Measles 8 5
Reporting 37 63
Total 100 100

Personnel dropped from 55 to 32 — not because anything new about personnel came in, but because reporting absorbed more of the rise.

Three quiet warnings

Warning 1 — Your prior matters

If Hiwot had started with “personnel never matters here” instead of “all three are equally likely”, the same Tuesday call would have moved her to a different place.

Different priors lead to different conclusions from the same evidence. That is not a bug — it is honest. The fix is to write down your prior so others can challenge it.

Warning 2 — Updating is not the same as overreacting

Each new piece of evidence shifts the picture. But evidence has weight, and small evidence should produce small shifts.

A single anecdote should not flip your belief from 33-33-33 to 5-5-90. If it did, your weights were wrong. Strong shifts require strong evidence.

Warning 3 — Rule 3 (colliders) catches almost everyone

Conditioning on a collider creates fake correlations between things that are actually unrelated.

If you find yourself surprised by a sudden correlation in your data, ask: did I just filter on a downstream collider? This is the error that hides inside half the famous “paradoxes” in epidemiology.

Try it yourself

You are the analyst

scenario

A regional director in Kenya sees that antenatal coverage in one county jumped from 65% to 78% in a single quarter. Three explanations sit on the table:

  1. The new SMS reminder programme is working.
  2. A coding change in DHIS2 reclassified some clinic visits.
  3. A measles vaccination drive brought more women to clinics, where they were also screened for ANC.

Start with 33-33-33. Then: a phone call confirms the DHIS2 coding change is real. How do your numbers move? What is the next piece of evidence you should ask for?

Hint: which one of the three explanations does the coding change support — and which does it weaken via explaining away?

Looking ahead

In Chapter 6, we will look at one of the strangest patterns in all of statistics: when the same data tells you opposite things at the country level and the regional level.

It has a name. Simpson’s Paradox. And it is closely related to the collider trap from Rule 3 above. We will see exactly how, and when to disaggregate, and when not to.

Further reading

The data behind Hiwot’s story

  • Federal Ministry of Health Ethiopia, Health Sector Transformation Plan II (2020/21–2024/25) — reporting pipeline reforms and quarterly review structure. Open-access.
  • DHS Ethiopia 2016, 2019 — regional-level maternal mortality estimates and trends. dhsprogram.com.
  • Croicu M. et al., 2017 — Reporting bias in routine health information systems. WHO Bulletin, 95(7). Open-access.

If you want to go deeper

  • Ryall, M. D. & Bramson, A. L. (2014) — Inference and Intervention. Routledge. Chapter 6 covers belief updating with the same lookup-table machinery from our Chapter 4.
  • McGrayne, S. B. (2011) — The Theory That Would Not Die. The history of Bayesian updating, told as a story. Surprisingly readable.

The one thing to remember

Bayesian updating is just redistributing your “out of 100” between explanations — keeping the total at 100 — based on which ones the new evidence fits.

Hiwot did not throw out her picture when new evidence arrived. She updated the numbers on it. That is what an analyst does all day.
